about: SHIP UPGRADES, 793-1066: forty things that can be fitted to a ship or done for her, each true to the period, with its evidence (Design/ship_upgrades.md is the one-page reading). This is the home CHAINS.md and unlocks_793.json name for the flags unlock_upgrade_<id>: the nine ids already in unlocks_793.json (sounding_line, iron_anchor, walrus_rope, tilt, new_sail, beitass, washstrake, ships_boat, half_deck) and the chain reward ice_chest keep their ids and their meaning here; where a price differs, the note says so. Evidence is taken from Design/content/ships.md (its source keys in square brackets), Design/ship_physics.md and six Wikipedia pages read on 6 Oct 2026 (named in each source). (D) = derived or judged by me; (?) = not checked against a source; LATER = the evidence is later than the year it is offered, or later than 1066. Not offered, because the period did not have them: a compass, a rudder on the sternpost, a chart, a crow's nest, a pump, a fore-and-aft sail, a second mast, a cannon. The sunstone is here only as a legend, and does nothing sure. A draft in the game's own file, for the user to overwrite. Written 6 Oct 2026.

units.id: the flag is unlock_upgrade_<id>, set on the one ship it is fitted to
units.group: speed, safety, cargo, crew or show (the groups of Design/ship_upgrades.md)
units.from, to: the years it can be had (793 = from the start, 1066 = to the end)
units.where: sites = the site kinds of BRIEF.md whose act:fit_upgrade offers it; ports = port ids of ports_793.json, an empty list meaning any port with such a site. Dorestad falls away after 863
units.cost_d: pennies, for a boat of the Gislinge's size (7.7 m, a sail of 10 m2). For bigger hulls see rules. goods = units of goods_793.json that are taken in place of part of the silver, where the fitting is made of a traded good
units.days: days she lies at the yard (the clock runs; the crew are fed). 0 = done within the four hours of act:fit_upgrade
units.fits: ship ids of story/ships_793.json, or all
units.effect: changes = a list of {field, by} (added to the class field) or {field, times} (multiplied), in the fields of ship_classes_793.json; plain = what else it does, in words, where there is no field. Every number is a starting guess to tune
units.upkeep: what it costs to keep, in words; due at the winter reckoning with the ship's own upkeep
units.lost_when: wreck (with the ship) | season (it must be done again each year) | years N (it wears out) | a named mishap | never
units.how_had: bought | reward (only by its flag from a chain or a card) | both. reward_note says which chain sets the flag today, or proposes what kind of chain should

rules: One fitting of each id to a ship. A fitting belongs to the hull: it is sold with her, inherited with her and lost with her in a wreck, unless lost_when says it can be carried to the next hull (a chest, a sounding line, a vane, a boat).
Size (D): cost_d and days are for a boat under 9 m. Times 2 for a hull of 9 to 12 m, times 4 for 13 to 17 m, times 8 above that. The fittings marked size_free cost the same on any hull.

Effects that change the same field add up, but no ship is bettered by more than a fifth in speed, 8 degrees toward the wind, or 0.25 in gale_fragility by fittings alone (D). A boat stays a boat: the way to a better ship is another ship (ships_793.json).
A fitting that needs a man (the tacking spar, the sounding line, more oars) does nothing when she is below crew_min plus one.
Nothing is fitted on a Sunday or a feast at a Christian port (town_actions_793.json fit_upgrade).
Upkeep unpaid for two winters: the fitting is gone (rope rots, tar dries, a sail goes thin).
Odds are words. Where an effect says one step better, it means doubtful to likely, or likely to sure, on the named check.

upgrades.name: A new sail of better wool
upgrades.what_it_is: A square sail of long-haired wool, spun hard and woven tight, in lengths sewn edge to edge. After the hull it is the dearest thing aboard, and it is women's winter work.
upgrades.evidence: Ottar's sail: 90 m2 from the wool of 200 old-breed sheep, about 1.1 kg a square metre [VSM-Ottar]. Roar Ege's hand-woven sail and rope took 5,000 of her 20,000 hours, and the sail of 1985 outlived the ship [EXARC] [VSM-Estrid]. No whole sail of these years survives; pieces of sailcloth were found reused in the roof of Trondenes church (LATER) (?).
upgrades.goods: 6 sailcloth in place of the silver

effect.plain: She is quicker on every point of sail and holds a little higher. A thin old sail (after eight years) gives these back.

upgrades.upkeep: none beyond drying it; dressing it is its own entry (sail_dressed)
upgrades.lost_when: years 8 (it is an old sail again); wreck; a torn-sail result in a gale costs a third of the price to mend
upgrades.reward_note: Set today by the winter card harbour.winter.weaving (winter_793.json): a winter of the house's own looms. Price: unlocks_793.json asks six units of sailcloth; 120 d is the same in silver (D) from 100 to 130 hours a square metre (ships.md 7.2).

upgrades.name: The sail dressed with fat and ochre
upgrades.what_it_is: Wool cloth lets the wind through. Rubbed with a wash of ochre and horse fat, and smoothed with a glass stone, it closes up and holds the wind. It also turns the sail a red-brown.
upgrades.evidence: The cloth of Ottar's sail was dressed with ochre and with horse-mane fat in water, rubbed in with glass smoothing stones [VSM-Ottar]. Glass linen-smoothers are common finds in the towns of the north (?). That sails of 793 were dressed this way is the museum's reconstruction, not a find (?).

effect.plain: A sail that does not drink the rain: no speed is lost in a wet sail on a day of rain.

upgrades.upkeep: done again every second spring, 6 d and two dry days ashore
upgrades.lost_when: years 2

upgrades.name: A tacking spar
upgrades.what_it_is: An ash pole that pushes the weather edge of the square sail forward, so the ship can work closer to the wind. One man tends it.
upgrades.evidence: The Norse word beitiass is written down only after 1066 (LATER). The replicas of the Skuldelev ships are not sailed to windward without it, and blocks with sockets for the spar's heel are read into the Skuldelev hulls (?). When it came into use is not known: 850 is a guess (?).

effect.plain: Only while a man is spared to tend it. On the chart: a head wind costs a day less in every four.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: shown by a Norse steersman at the end of a chain sailed in his company. unlocks_793.json asks tongue.old_norse >= 0.5 to buy it.
upgrades.source: unlocks_793.json unlock_upgrade_beitass; Viking Ship Museum sailing trials (ships.md 5.1)

upgrades.name: Reef bands and a net of lines on the sail
upgrades.what_it_is: Rows of short cords sewn across the sail so its foot can be tied up and the sail made smaller in a rising wind, and a net of light lines on its fore side to keep the cloth from bagging.
upgrades.evidence: The Gotland picture stones of the eighth and ninth centuries show sails covered with a diamond net of lines, with many lines led down to the crew (?). Reef points on a sail of these years are reconstructed, not found (ship_physics.md 1.5).

effect.plain: In a rising wind she may go on under a small sail at half speed, where without it the choice is only to strike sail and row, or to run.

upgrades.lost_when: with the sail (years 8, or a torn sail)
upgrades.source: ship_physics.md 1.5 and 2.10 (reefing); the picture stones from memory (?)

upgrades.name: Another pair of oars, and two spare
upgrades.what_it_is: Oars of pine or ash, cut to her length, with new thole pins and grommets of withy at the gunwale, and two spare lashed under the thwarts.
upgrades.evidence: Sea Stallion's oars took 35 pines (ships.md 7.1). The Gislinge boat rows three pairs [VSM-Lang]; a boat of her length can seat a fourth at the cost of cargo room (D). Oars lie in the Oseberg and Gokstad burials, the Oseberg ones new-made and some unfinished (?).

effect.plain: Only with two more men than crew_min to pull them. A broken-oar result costs nothing while a spare is aboard.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; a spare is used up by each broken-oar result
upgrades.source: ships.md 4.3, 7.1; the Oseberg oars from memory (?)

upgrades.name: Hauled out, scraped and tarred
upgrades.what_it_is: She is drawn up, the weed and shell scraped off, the seams and the whole hull painted with hot pine tar inside and out. A clean tarred hull slips through the water and drinks none.
upgrades.evidence: Sea Stallion took 600 litres of tar [VSM-SeaSt]. The museum's boats are hauled out at the end of October and tarred over the winter [EXARC]. Tar was made in great funnel pits in the Swedish forests from the eighth century, far beyond a farm's own need: read as tar for ships and sails (Hennius 2018, from memory (?)). goods_793.json has tar and pitch.

effect.plain: The base leak is halved for the year. A ship not tarred for two years loses the same again below her table speeds (D). The currach takes grease and tallow on her hides instead, at the same price.

upgrades.upkeep: this is upkeep: it is done again each winter
upgrades.lost_when: season
upgrades.source: ships.md 7.1, 7.3; act:careen in town_actions_793.json is the same work and should give this

upgrades.name: A tow mast and a long line
upgrades.what_it_is: A short stout mast stepped well forward, and a long line of bast to the bank. Men or oxen on the towpath pull; the line leads high so it clears the reeds, and the boat steers herself off the bank.
upgrades.evidence: Utrecht 1 has a small mast step near the bow, read as a step for a towing mast (ship_physics.md 1.5) [MASS-Utr]. Towing upriver by men is told of the Rhine in these years: the boatmen who hauled against the stream are in the Miracles of St Goar (ninth century) (?).

effect.plain: A keel boat without the field is towed at 14 km a day with it (D), where she rowed at half that. Haulers are still hired by the day (act:hire_porters).

upgrades.upkeep: a new line every third year, 5 d
upgrades.lost_when: wreck

upgrades.name: Rollers and hauling tackle
upgrades.what_it_is: Six logs of peeled ash, two long ropes and a pair of shoulder yokes. With them a crew can drag a boat over a bar, up a beach above the storm line, or across a neck of land from one water to the next.
upgrades.evidence: The Kanhave canal on Samso was cut in 726 to pass ships across the island [Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen, class table]. Constantine VII, about 950, tells how the Rus drag and carry their boats past the Dnieper rapids (De Administrando Imperio 9) (?). The land crossing from the Schlei to the Treene behind Hedeby is believed, and no slipway has been found (?).

effect.plain: A portage marked on the chart can be crossed: a day for each kilometre with her cargo carried (D). Hauling her above the tide line takes an hour, not half a day, so a gale ashore is sure to find her safe.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; left behind if she must be lightened

upgrades.name: New caulking of tarred wool
upgrades.what_it_is: A cord of spun wool or twisted cattle hair, soaked in tar, is laid in every plank lap as it is riveted. On an old hull the worst seams are opened and laid again.
upgrades.evidence: Estrid Byrding, the new Skuldelev 3 of 2022, is caulked with tarred three-strand wool yarn, as the wreck was [VSM-Estrid]. Wikipedia, Viking ship: a caulking of tarred rope between the planks (read 6 Oct 2026).
upgrades.goods: 1 tar and 1 raw_wool in place of 12 d

effect.plain: Fewer leaks: the leak when she works in a sea is halved, so one man less bails and cargo low in the hold stays dry.

upgrades.upkeep: none for six years, then again
upgrades.lost_when: years 6; a grounding on hard ground opens it

upgrades.name: New moss, laths and clamps
upgrades.what_it_is: The seams of a flat river craft are packed with moss, a thin lath is laid over it, and the lath is held down by small iron clamps driven in a row. It lasts a year or two and is then done again.
upgrades.evidence: The barges of the Rhine delta are caulked with moss under laths, held with iron caulking clamps (sintels); Vleuten 2 has no other iron in her [BJM]. The Slav boats of the Baltic are pegged with treenails and caulked with moss (ships.md 2.5).

effect.plain: Fewer leaks and a drier cargo: grain and salt on the bottom boards do not spoil for bilge water this year. Left undone, a tenth of a low-stowed cargo that fears wet is spoiled on a voyage of more than ten days (D).

upgrades.upkeep: this is upkeep: done again each spring
upgrades.lost_when: season

upgrades.name: A spare steering oar and withy
upgrades.what_it_is: The steering oar hangs on the right side aft by a twisted band of withy or hide through a wooden boss, with a tiller across the boat. The band is the weak thing in a ship. A second oar and two bands, ready cut, lie under the stern.
upgrades.evidence: Gokstad: a quarter rudder fastened to a large block of wood outside the hull and supported by an extra stout rib (Wikipedia, Gokstad ship, read 6 Oct 2026). Oseberg: a broad steering oar (Wikipedia, Oseberg Ship). Kvalsund, 780-800: a detachable rudder on one side (ship_physics.md 1.5). A rudder alone was found at Vorsaa in Jutland (?).

effect.plain: A steering-gone result in a following sea costs an hour, not the day and the broach check. Grounding with the oar down breaks the band, not the oar.

upgrades.upkeep: a new band each spring, 1 d
upgrades.lost_when: used up by one steering-gone result; wreck

upgrades.name: A sounding line and lead
upgrades.what_it_is: A lead weight on a line knotted at every fathom. The hollow in its foot is armed with tallow, which brings up a pinch of the bottom: sand, shell or mud tells a seaman where he is when he cannot see. On the flats a marked pole does the same.
upgrades.evidence: Greek and Roman leads have been found; Acts 27.28 tells of sounding; the Bayeux Tapestry shows sounding at the landing of 1066; leads had a wad of tallow in a hollow at the bottom (Wikipedia, Sounding line, read 6 Oct 2026). Old English has sundgyrd, a sounding rod, and sundline (?). No lead from a ship of 793 in these waters is known to me (?).

effect.plain: In fog or at night within a day of a coast, grounding checks are one step better, and the fuzzy area of her place on the chart is halved near a bar she has sounded before. It needs a man in the bow.

upgrades.upkeep: a lump of tallow, nothing to count
upgrades.lost_when: never while a man swims ashore with it: it is carried to the next hull unless the wreck result says all was lost
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: a pilot's parting gift, or taken from a wreck card. unlocks_793.json asks two units of lead and 6 d.

upgrades.name: An iron anchor in place of the stone
upgrades.what_it_is: A small boat lies to a killick: a stone lashed in a frame of wood. An anchor forged of iron, with flukes, a wooden stock and a length of chain next to it, bites where a stone only drags.
upgrades.evidence: The Oseberg ship, buried in the autumn of 834, had an iron anchor (Wikipedia, Oseberg Ship, read 6 Oct 2026). The Ladby ship, early tenth century, had an anchor of about 20 kg, 1.26 m long, on a chain once about 11 m [da-Ladby] [WP-Long]. Stone anchors for small boats: ship_physics.md 1.5 (from memory (?)).

effect.plain: At anchor in a gale the drag check is one step better. She can lie off a beach she cannot be hauled up on, and wait outside a bar for the tide. On rock it holds no better than the stone.

upgrades.lost_when: cut away (the cut-and-run choice on a lee shore); wreck. Iron is worth stealing: a raid on the port may take it
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: the pay of a smith's chain (iron carried from the Rhine to a northern smith). Price: unlocks_793.json asks four units of bar iron and 60 d, which is this.
upgrades.source: unlocks_793.json unlock_upgrade_iron_anchor; ships.md 7.4; ship_physics.md 2.9 (holding by ground); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oseberg_Ship

upgrades.name: A second killick and a long cable
upgrades.what_it_is: A second anchor stone in its wooden frame, and a cable of lime bast long enough to lie at five times the depth. Two anchors spread ahead hold a boat in a tideway where one lets her swing ashore.
upgrades.evidence: Rope of lime bast and horsehair is the everyday kind on the Roskilde replicas [VSM-Ottar]. Stone anchors in wooden frames are the small boat's anchor through the whole period (?). That scope is what holds is plain seamanship (ship_physics.md 2.9).

effect.plain: A dragging-anchor result may be answered once with the second anchor at no cost. One anchor may be cut away without leaving her with none.

upgrades.upkeep: a new cable every fourth year, 6 d
upgrades.lost_when: cut away; wreck

upgrades.name: Rigging of walrus hide
upgrades.what_it_is: Rope cut in one long spiral strip from the hide of a walrus or a seal. It is the strongest rope in the north, and it is used for the shrouds, the stay and the halyard, where a parted rope brings the mast down.
upgrades.evidence: Ohthere told King Alfred about 890 that the Finnas paid tribute in ship's ropes of whale hide and seal hide, sixty ells long (the Old English Orosius; texts_793.json ohthere, Bosworth 1859) [WP-Oht]. Before 890 it is a northern thing, had only in Norse ports.
upgrades.where_note: from about 890 also at lundenwic, eoforwic, hamwic and duiblinn

effect.plain: Rigging does not part in a gale: the mast-gone result is one step less likely, and she can carry her sail a little longer in a strong wind. Used as the anchor cable, the cable does not part.

upgrades.upkeep: greased each winter with seal oil or tallow, 2 d; that hide rope goes slack when long wet is general knowledge of rawhide (?)
upgrades.lost_when: years 10; wreck
upgrades.reward_note: Set today by the finale of the chain walrus_ivory (Design/content/chains/walrus_ivory.md).

upgrades.name: Two good bailers and a bucket
upgrades.what_it_is: Scoops carved from one piece of wood with a handle behind, shaped to the curve of the bilge, and a stave-built bucket on a lanyard. A boat always has one bailer. Two, and a well cleared in the bottom boards to bail from, are the difference when she ships a sea.
upgrades.evidence: The Oseberg ship was buried with a bailer among her fittings (Wikipedia, Oseberg Ship, read 6 Oct 2026). Wooden bailers are common finds in Norse boat graves (ship_physics.md 1.5, from memory (?)). An open boat with 20 to 30 cm of water loose in her is close to capsizing even on flat water (ship_physics.md 1.6).

effect.plain: Two men can bail at once: the water-aboard check after a sea comes over is one step better. It is the cheapest thing in this file.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; one goes over the side now and then (a small sea card)

upgrades.name: Ballast stones
upgrades.what_it_is: Rounded stones laid low along the keel under the bottom boards. A ship with no cargo, or with a light cargo of fur and cloth, stands up to her sail only with weight in her. They are thrown out on the beach when a heavy cargo comes aboard.
upgrades.evidence: Vidfamne, the replica of the Askekarr ship, needs at least 7 t of ballast when light [sv-Ask]. Stones foreign to the shore lie in the harbours of the northern towns and are read as ballast thrown out (Kaupang, Hedeby) (?).

effect.plain: A switch, not a fitting: taken aboard or thrown out at any beach in an hour. It counts only when she is less than half laden. A heavy cargo stowed low (querns, iron, salt) is its own ballast and gives the same.

upgrades.lost_when: thrown out by choice; it is the first thing over the side when she must be lightened

upgrades.name: A stouter mast step and partner
upgrades.what_it_is: The mast stands in a block on the keel (the old woman, in the later Norse word) and is held at the height of the thwarts by a second great timber (the mast fish). On a boat it is a thwart with a clamp. Both are made new of grown oak, longer and thicker than before, to spread the mast's push over more ribs.
upgrades.evidence: The mast partner of the Oseberg ship had split and was mended with iron bands: her rig was too weak for the open sea (from memory (?)). The Gokstad ship, built of timber felled about 890, has a far heavier step and partner (Wikipedia, Gokstad ship: a picture of the mast step, no words on it; read 6 Oct 2026). Sea Stallion took three oaks for the keelson and mast fish [VSM-SeaSt].

effect.plain: She may carry sail one step of wind longer before the mast is at risk. The hull works less at the mast, so the seams there stay tight.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck
upgrades.source: ships.md 7.1 (Sea Stallion); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gokstad_ship; the Oseberg mast partner from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A strake added
upgrades.what_it_is: The wright scarfs a new plank along each side above the old top strake and raises the tholes to it. She sits the same in the water, carries more, and takes less sea over the side. She also rows heavier and catches more wind.
upgrades.evidence: Skuldelev 6 was rebuilt from a fishing boat into a carrier with a raised side and fewer oars (ships.md 7.4 (?)). Adding or renewing strakes is ordinary clinker practice; Skuldelev 3 was mended with lengths of plank let in [EXARC].

effect.plain: The one fitting that makes the first boat a bigger boat: the Gislinge goes from 660 to about 790 kg. Only hulls of 12 m or less, or the two logboat kinds. Days do not scale with size: it is a winter's work whatever she is.

upgrades.upkeep: the ship's own upkeep rises by a tenth
upgrades.lost_when: wreck
upgrades.reward_note: Set today by the winter card harbour.winter.rebuild (winter_793.json), at 200 d while wintering.

upgrades.name: Shutters for the oar ports
upgrades.what_it_is: On a ship whose oars pass through holes in the side, each hole gets a round wooden lid on a peg that is turned across it when the oars are in. Without them she takes water at every hole when she heels.
upgrades.evidence: Gokstad: the oar holes could be hatched down when the ship was under sail (Wikipedia, Gokstad ship, read 6 Oct 2026). The Oseberg ship has oar holes and no shutters (?).

effect.plain: She may be sailed hard on the wind without the low side filling. From 850 as a guess: the first hull known to have them was built about 890.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck

upgrades.name: A boat towed astern
upgrades.what_it_is: A four-oar boat on a line behind the ship, or turned over on the cargo in a hard blow. It lands men and goods on a beach the ship cannot reach, carries an anchor out to haul her off a bank, and is the last hope when she fills.
upgrades.evidence: The Gokstad grave held three small boats beside the ship (Wikipedia, Gokstad ship, read 6 Oct 2026) [VSM-Joanna]. ships.md 4.2: the four-oar boat is the ship's boat of a knarr.

effect.plain: She can trade at a beach landing she cannot reach herself. Off a bank: the kedge choice is open (an hour, likely). In a wreck the men are likely saved, not doubtful. She tows it at a small cost in speed.

upgrades.lost_when: a gale at sea is likely to take it unless it was got aboard; it is not lost with the ship: the crew come home in it
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: left to the house by a skipper it saved. Price: unlocks_793.json says 250 d; ships.md 8.2 puts a four-oar boat at 80 to 120 d new, and west_small_boat is 150 d in ships_793.json, so 120 d is offered here (D).

upgrades.name: New rivets and roves
upgrades.what_it_is: Iron rivets rust thin, first below the water. In her fifteenth year the wright draws the worst and drives new ones over new roves, strake by strake. It is the refit that gives an old hull her second life.
upgrades.evidence: Roar Ege took 648 new rivets and 142 new spikes in 31 years, half her rivets over again; the modern rivets need replacing after about 15 years, sooner below the waterline [EXARC]. A rivet with its rove is about 50 g of iron (ships.md 7.2). Iron rivets lie in the Frisian terps, 400 to 800 [BJM].

effect.plain: Offered only on a hull of 12 years or more. Her age for leaks and for the end of her life is set back ten years; without it she is worth only her timber at life_years. The price is a tenth of her own cost_d, whatever she is (ships.md 7.3): 60 d is the Gislinge's.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; once in a hull's life

upgrades.name: A tent for the nights
upgrades.what_it_is: A tent of cloth stretched over the boat on a frame of crossed boards when she lies at anchor or on a beach. It keeps the rain off the men and off the cargo beneath them.
upgrades.evidence: The Gokstad grave held a tent (Wikipedia, Gokstad ship, read 6 Oct 2026). The Oseberg grave had tent frames with carved boards (from memory (?): the article read does not name them). ships.md 7.4: a tent and a cooking kettle for nights ashore.
upgrades.goods: 2 sailcloth, or 2 wadmal, in place of the silver

effect.plain: The crew's health does not fall for cold or rain on nights aboard or on a beach, and no lodging is paid where there is a beach. Cargo is not spoiled by rain while she lies still.

upgrades.lost_when: years 10; a gale ashore may take it; wreck

upgrades.name: Greased hides over the hold
upgrades.what_it_is: Cattle hides or seal skins sewn edge to edge and rubbed with fat, lashed down over the cargo amidships on a ridge pole. Spray and rain run off into the bilge.
upgrades.evidence: An open hold needs a cover to carry cloth, fur or grain at all; hides and skins are trade goods of every port in goods_793.json. Skin covers over a knarr's cargo are told in the sagas (LATER) (?). No cover has been found with a wreck (?).
upgrades.goods: 2 cattle_hides or 2 seal_skins in place of the silver

effect.plain: A drier cargo: spoilage by spray and rain at sea is halved for goods that fear wet (grain, flour, salt, cloth, fur, books). With decks fore and aft as well, it is quartered.

upgrades.lost_when: years 6; wreck; cut up to patch a stove plank (a choice on a damage card)
upgrades.source: goods_793.json cattle_hides, seal_skins; the sagas from memory (?)

upgrades.name: Decks fore and aft
upgrades.what_it_is: Loose deck planks laid on the beams at bow and stern, with an open hold between. The men stand and work on the decks; the best goods lie dry under them.
upgrades.evidence: Skuldelev 1 (about 1030) and Skuldelev 3 (about 1040) are decked fore and aft over an open hold [VSM-S1]. 990 is a guess at when a trader was first built so: the Klaastad ship of about that year is the earliest hull read as a pure cargo carrier (?).

effect.plain: A drier cargo: spoilage by spray and rain halved. A fifth of her hold (D) is under the decks and takes no harm at all: put the cloth, fur and books there. Times 4 for her size makes 300 d on a 14 m ship, as unlocks_793.json has it.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck

upgrades.name: Brushwood under the cargo
upgrades.what_it_is: A bed of hazel rods and birch brush laid over the bottom boards before the cargo goes in. Bilge water runs under it, and stone or iron cannot chafe through the planks.
upgrades.evidence: The Klaastad ship, wrecked about 990 near Kaupang with a cargo of whetstone blanks, had a layer of hazel branches under the cargo (from memory (?)). The Graveney boat of about 950 had hops and quern pieces on her bottom [MASS].

effect.plain: A drier cargo from below: no spoilage by bilge water. Loading querns, millstones or bar iron does no harm to the hull (without it, a doubtful chance of a sprung plank in a gale with stone aboard).

upgrades.upkeep: cut new each spring: an hour and a penny
upgrades.lost_when: season
upgrades.source: ships.md 2.2 (Graveney); the Klaastad dunnage from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A lock chest
upgrades.what_it_is: An oak chest bound with iron, with a spring lock and a key the skipper wears. It is lashed to a rib under the stern. The silver, the scales, the charter and the letters go in it.
upgrades.evidence: Chests with iron locks lay in the Oseberg burial of 834 (?). The Mastermyr chest from Gotland, about 1000, is an oak chest with a lock, found full of a smith's tools (?). Keys and padlocks are among the commonest iron finds at Hedeby, Birka and York (?).

effect.plain: Theft cards in harbour and thieving by a hired man are one step better for the house. Letters and a charter are dry and are saved in a wreck if the men are. A raider takes it first: it does nothing against force.

upgrades.lost_when: taken by raiders who board her; carried to the next hull otherwise
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: found with its key lost at the end of a chain, with something in it.
upgrades.source: the Oseberg and Mastermyr chests and the town finds, all from memory (?)

upgrades.name: Hurdles and a ramp for beasts
upgrades.what_it_is: Wattle hurdles lashed across the hold to pen cattle, sheep or horses standing, head to the side, with a slatted ramp to walk them aboard over the gunwale from a beach.
upgrades.evidence: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 892: the great army crossed from Boulogne to the Lympne mouth with horses and all, in 250 ships (Giles 1847). The Bayeux Tapestry shows horses standing in the open ships of 1066 and stepping out over the side (?). The museum's tonne for the Gislinge boat is four men and ten sheep (ships_793.json).

effect.plain: She may load the living goods (sheep, pigs; cattle and horses on a hull of 10 m or more). Without it a beast aboard is a doubtful check each day at sea. Beasts need water and fodder from the stores.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; burnt for firewood on a cold beach (a choice)
upgrades.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 892 (Giles 1847); ships_793.json gislinge; the Tapestry from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A cabin on a river ship
upgrades.what_it_is: A small house of boards and hides built on the hull, with a door and a bench. A man of rank travels in it, out of the rain and out of sight of the crew.
upgrades.evidence: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, chapter 7: in 826 the bishop of Cologne gave Harald and Anskar a good boat for the Rhine journey to Dorestad in which two cabins had been made; Harald took one and Anskar the other (Robinson 1921).

effect.plain: She may carry a passenger of rank (a bishop, an abbot, a count's man): the passenger cards pay double and raise standing with his lord. Books and church goods travel dry in it.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; a gale on open water is likely to take it (she is a river ship)
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: built at a bishop's cost for the house that carries him, in a chain on the Rhine.

upgrades.name: A chest of cold
upgrades.what_it_is: A double chest packed with winter ice in moss and straw. Fish, butter and a dead man keep in it far longer than they should.
upgrades.evidence: Wulfstan told King Alfred that among the Este there is a people who can make cold: the dead lie unburnt for a month or two and do not rot, and they can freeze a vessel of ale or water in summer as in winter (the Old English Orosius). How they did it is not told. Winter ice kept in straw is ordinary; the rest is the least sure thing in this file (?).

effect.plain: One unit of a good that spoils (fresh fish, butter, eels, whale meat) keeps twice as long, from a port with winter ice and until about midsummer.

upgrades.upkeep: new ice each winter, where there is ice
upgrades.lost_when: wreck; useless after midsummer until the next frost
upgrades.reward_note: Set today by the finale E2 of the chain amber_road (Design/content/chains/amber_road.md), at 60 d, and nowhere else.
upgrades.source: Design/content/chains/amber_road.md; Wulfstan in the Old English Orosius, as that chain reads it (?)

upgrades.name: A kettle, a tripod and a hearth box
upgrades.what_it_is: An iron kettle on a chain and a three-legged stand for the beach, and a shallow box of sand and flat stones in which a small fire of charcoal can be kept alive at anchor in still water. At sea under way no fire is lit: the food is cold.
upgrades.evidence: A riveted iron cauldron with its tripod and chain lay in the Oseberg burial of 834 (from memory (?): the article read does not list the kitchen gear). ships.md 7.4: a cooking kettle for nights ashore. A fire box aboard is not attested by any find of these years: it is offered as a thing for harbour and anchor only (?).

effect.plain: Hot food on every night ashore or at anchor: morale does not fall for cold food, and health mends a step faster on a beach. Stores go a tenth further (porridge from meal, in place of bread).

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; sold in need (it is 2 units of iron tools' worth)
upgrades.source: ships.md 7.4; the Oseberg cauldron from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A sea chest for each man
upgrades.what_it_is: A low chest with a sloped lid for every man, wide at the foot so it does not slide. He sits on it to row and keeps his own things in it: his cloak, his knife, and the little he trades for himself.
upgrades.evidence: The Oseberg and Gokstad ships have no fixed benches for the rowers: the men are taken to have sat on their own chests (?). Chests of the right height were found at Oseberg (?). A crew that trades on its own account is the felag of the rune stones (research_scale_to_fleets.md).
upgrades.cost_note: 5 d a man: 20 d for the Gislinge's four

effect.plain: Each man may carry a little of his own to sell: morale up, a man is one step less likely to leave at a rich port, and hired men ask a tenth less. On a hull with oar ports it is also his rowing seat.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck (and the men remember what they lost)
upgrades.source: the Oseberg and Gokstad chests from memory (?); Design/research_scale_to_fleets.md (felag)

upgrades.name: Skin sleeping bags
upgrades.what_it_is: A bag of sheepskin or hide, hair inside, big enough for two men. By day it holds their gear and keeps it dry; by night they sleep in it between the ribs.
upgrades.evidence: The Old Norse hudfat, a hide bag a seaman sleeps in and stows his things in, is in the sagas and the sea laws (LATER) (?). Nothing of the kind has been found from these years (?). Sheepskins and hides are in every market (goods_793.json).
upgrades.cost_note: 4 d for each two men: 8 d for the Gislinge
upgrades.goods: 1 fleeces for each two men in place of the silver

effect.plain: Health does not fall for cold on a night at sea before the feast of St Martin; after it, one step less. A crew with them will sail a week earlier in spring and a week later in autumn without grumbling.

upgrades.lost_when: years 5; wreck
upgrades.source: the word from memory, LATER (?); goods_793.json fleeces

upgrades.name: Water casks and a dipper
upgrades.what_it_is: Two stave-built casks of fresh water, bunged and lashed at the mast, and a wooden dipper on a cord. A small boat carries a skin or a pail and must land every day or two to fill it.
upgrades.evidence: Stave-built vessels are ordinary: the yew bucket of the Oseberg burial is held with brass strips (Wikipedia, Oseberg Ship, read 6 Oct 2026). Wine casks of silver fir from the upper Rhine were reused as well linings at Dorestad (?). That a crossing needs water for its days is plain.

effect.plain: She can stay at sea six days without landing for water, where she had two (D). An empty wine cask from her own cargo serves as well.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; stove in by a shifting cargo in a gale (doubtful)
upgrades.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oseberg_Ship; the Dorestad cask wells from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A gangplank
upgrades.what_it_is: A long plank with steps cut across it and a hole at the head for a line. Laid from the gunwale to a jetty or a beach, it lets a cask be rolled and a man walk loaded.
upgrades.evidence: The Oseberg ship was buried with her gangplank among the fittings (Wikipedia, Oseberg Ship, read 6 Oct 2026). The Gokstad ship had one too (?).

effect.plain: Loading and unloading (act:load) takes half the time, and one porter less is hired. Casks are not dropped (a small harbour card it turns off).

upgrades.lost_when: wreck

upgrades.name: A carved stem
upgrades.what_it_is: The stem head is carved: a spiral, a beast's head, a band of gripping beasts down the stem. On a small boat it is a plain scroll with a painted eye. A head that can be lifted off its tenon is taken down when she comes into a friend's water.
upgrades.evidence: The stem of the Oseberg ship, buried 834, ends in a spiral with a serpent's head and is carved with beasts along its length (?). Carved animal-head posts dredged from the Scheldt are dated to the fifth to seventh centuries (?). The Icelandic law that a ship must take off her gaping heads in sight of land, so as not to frighten the land spirits, is written down after 1066 (LATER).

effect.plain: She has a face and a name: she is known again in every port she has called at (standing rises a little faster, good and bad). The crew's morale is a step higher in a hard hour. A beast's head left up in a Christian or a wary port makes the first greeting a step colder: taking it down is a choice at the harbour mouth.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; an heir may have it set on the next hull if she was not lost
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: cut by a named carver as his thanks at the end of a chain: the house's own beast.
upgrades.source: the Oseberg stem, the Scheldt heads and the Icelandic law, all from memory (?)

upgrades.name: A gilded vane
upgrades.what_it_is: A quarter-round plate of gilt bronze, pierced and engraved with a great beast, with a small cast beast standing on its top edge and a row of holes along the curve for streamers. It stands on the stem head or the mast top of a great man's ship and shows the wind.
upgrades.evidence: The Soderala vane of gilt bronze is dated to about 1050 by its style and is thought to have been made as a weather vane for a Viking ship, likely a large one; it shows long use aboard (Wikipedia, Soderala vane, read 6 Oct 2026). The vanes of Kallunge, Heggen and Tingelstad are of the same century or a little later (?). Before about 1000 none is known: a merchant of 793 shows the wind with a strip of cloth on the stay.

effect.plain: A lord's ship is known by it from far off: standing with kings and jarls a step higher, tolls asked more politely, and a raider thinks twice (she looks like a great man's ship) or wants it badly (it is gold to look at). The wind's turn is seen a little sooner.

upgrades.lost_when: taken by raiders who board her; it is unshipped and carried to the next hull otherwise
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: a king's gift at the end of a late chain (after 1000), never an early one.
upgrades.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Söderala_vane; the other vanes from memory (?)

upgrades.name: Shields along the rail
upgrades.what_it_is: A batten along the outside of the top strake, with the crew's shields tied to it rim over rim when she lies in harbour or rows into a strange one. It is for show: under sail in a sea they are taken in.
upgrades.evidence: The Gokstad ship was buried with her shields hung along both sides on a shield rack, painted by turns yellow and black, thirty-two a side (from memory (?): the article read on 6 Oct 2026 does not describe them). Ships with a row of shields are on the Gotland picture stones (?).
upgrades.goods: the shields themselves: 1 shields for each four men, bought as goods

effect.plain: She looks armed: a lone raider's choice to chase is one step less likely, and in a boarding the crew are one step better off. A king's man and a toll man are a step colder to a trader who comes in dressed for war, and in a peace-holy market the shields must come down.

upgrades.lost_when: wreck; the shields are goods and may be sold
upgrades.source: the Gokstad shields and the picture stones from memory (?); goods_793.json shields

upgrades.name: A sail of two colours
upgrades.what_it_is: The lengths of the sail are dyed by turns, or strips of a second colour are sewn on in a pattern of squares: madder red and undyed white, or woad blue and white.
upgrades.evidence: The sails on the Gotland picture stones are chequered in diamonds (?). The Encomium Emmae, written 1041-42, tells of the painted and coloured ships and sails of Cnut's fleet (?). The Bayeux Tapestry stitches the sails of 1066 in stripes (?). goods_793.json has madder and woad.
upgrades.goods: 1 madder or 1 woad in place of 20 d

effect.plain: She is known from as far as her sail is seen. Friends, factors and partners know her before she lands (the port is ready: half a day saved where the house has a man). So do those who owe her a grudge: a raider she has met before knows her too. Her own other keels find her at a meeting place more surely.

upgrades.lost_when: with the sail
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: the colours a lord or a guild of merchants grants the house to sail under.
upgrades.source: the picture stones, the Encomium Emmae and the Tapestry, all from memory (?); goods_793.json madder, woad

upgrades.name: A sunstone (a tale)
upgrades.what_it_is: A clear stone that a Northman says shows where the sun stands behind cloud when it is turned in the hand. He will sell it. Whether it does anything is not known, and the game does not say.
upgrades.evidence: LEGEND. The only text that tells of its use is the tale of Raudulf, of the thirteenth or fourteenth century, in which a king finds the sun in an overcast sky with it. Other mentions are in thirteenth-century sagas and in church inventories of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. That it was a tool of seamen is a modern guess; trials at sea in 2014 failed (Wikipedia, Sunstone (medieval), read 6 Oct 2026). The wooden half-disc from Uunartoq in Greenland, about 1000, has been read as a sun dial for holding a course, and that too is disputed (?).

effect.plain: Nothing sure. No check is bettered and the chart shows nothing new. A crew who believe in it (heathen Norse men aboard) keep their morale one step longer in fog; a priest aboard thinks less of the skipper. It can be sold on, given as a gift a Northman values, or kept for the tale.

upgrades.lost_when: never, unless given, sold or sunk
upgrades.reward_note: Proposed: the small prize of a northern chain, given with a straight face.

needs: unlocks_793.json and town_actions_793.json (fit_upgrade) say the fittings move here if this file comes: whoever owns them should point act:fit_upgrade at this file and drop the nine upgrade entries there, or keep them as the offers (when, cost in the engine's grammar) and read name, evidence and effect from here.
Prices that differ from unlocks_793.json: ships_boat 250 d there, 120 d here; half_deck 300 d there, 75 d x 4 for size here (the same on a 14 m ship). All others agree.
No engine variable reads a fitting today except flag.unlock_upgrade_<id>. The effects are rules for a programmer, not wired.
act:careen should set tar_coat for the year; the winter cards harbour.winter.weaving and harbour.winter.rebuild already set new_sail and washstrake.
Goods used as part payment exist in goods_793.json: sailcloth, tar, raw_wool, lead, bar_iron, rope, walrus_rope, rivets, cattle_hides, seal_skins, wadmal, fleeces, shields, madder, woad.

Checked on 6 Oct 2026 by script: 40 entries, every fits id is a ship of story/ships_793.json, every port a port of ports_793.json, every site a site kind of BRIEF.md, every changed field a field of ship_classes_793.json.
